Red List Authority Coordinator: Johannes Penner (email: johannes.penner@web.de)

actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species ranges from Guinea to Togo (Chippaux 2006) occuring from sea level up to 1,520 m.
documentation.population: This snake can be locally abundant, with as many as 282 individuals recorded within a few square kilometres in Côte d'Ivoire (Doucet 1963, Penner et al. 2008). A population density of 0.053 animals per hectare, low for a large viper, was calculated during a recent study of Taï National Park, however, the authors caution that recapture rates were too low to derive a robust estimate (Penner et al. 2008). The species' population status is otherwise unstudied and reliable estimates are difficult to derive due to the snakes' cryptic habits (Penner et al. 2008).
documentation.habitats: This nocturnal snake is found in moist Guinean savanna, humid forest and  anthropogenic habitats, including both subsistence and agro-industrial  plantations, and is not uncommon in towns (Chippaux 2006). It is viviparous,  giving birth to 13-15 young (Chippaux 2006). It also occurs at forest edges (W.R. Branch pers. comm. 2012).
documentation.threats: It is subject to forest degradation due to deforestation and use by locals; as this snake has broad habitat tolerances these activities are not considered to be affecting the global population significantly.
documentation.measures: It is present in many protected areas.
documentation.use_trade: This snake is used as food and for leather, and is likely to be used for local medicinal purposes. It is found in the international pet trade and (as B. gabonica rhinoceros) was among the non-CITES reptile species that commanded the highest prices in the European Union in the 1990s (Auliya 2003).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern as this species is widespread, can be locally common, and is adaptable and not subject to major threats.
